newsitem.title: USA: CALIF. APPEALS COURT STAYS RELEASE OF TRANSCRIPTS.
newsitem.headline: CALIF. APPEALS COURT STAYS RELEASE OF TRANSCRIPTS.

text.p: A California appeals court Wednesday stayed a lower court's decision ordering the release of grand jury transcripts about Merrill Lynch and Co's role in the Orange County bankruptcy.

"The trial court's order unsealing the grand jury transcripts and opening the transcripts for public inspection is stayed pending further order of this court," a three-judge panel of the California Court of Appeal, 4th Appellate District, Division Three in Santa Ana said in a short, written order.
The court said "any interested party" may file a reply on the issue of the stay by next Tuesday.

The decision was handed down soon after Merrill Lynch filed a notice of appeal and a request for an emergency stay of a ruling made a few hours earlier by Orange County Superior Court Judge David Carter.

Carter had ordered the immediate release of grand jury transcripts that may shed light on Merrill Lynch's role in the bankruptcy crisis. Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after losing more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. It emerged from bankruptcy last year.
In June, Merrill Lynch settled with Orange County's district attorney for $30 million, ensuring that the brokerage giant and its employees would not face criminal charges.

Lawyers for Orange County and news organizations asked Carter to give them access to the sealed grand jury transcripts. County attorneys said the transcripts could bolster their $2 billion-plus lawsuit against Merrill Lynch.
The suit alleges Merrill Lynch sold Orange County risky securities in violation of the law. Merrill Lynch has denied any wrongdoing and is contesting the allegations in court.

County prosecutors and Merrill Lynch had argued that the transcripts should remain sealed because no indictments were returned by the grand jury. In a court filing last month, Merrill Lynch asked Carter to keep the transcripts sealed to protect proprietary information about the company and safeguard the reputations of its employees.

But Carter ruled that: "The public, our state and federal elected officials and the financial community must be allowed access to information that allows them to examine the events that led to the largest municipal bankruptcy in our nation's history."
